standard_text: Convert between any two representations (fractions, decimals, percents) of positive rational numbers without the use of a calculator.

skills.name: Identify fractions on tenths and hundredths grids

prerequisite_skill.description: Write decimals as fractions with denominators 10 or 100.

skills.i_do_script: A tenths grid has 10 equal parts. Each column is one-tenth. A hundredths grid has 100 equal squares. Count the shaded sections to find the numerator, and the total sections to find the denominator.

canonical_error.pattern: Counts grid lines instead of shaded columns or squares.
canonical_error.example: Counts 3 shading boundaries and thinks it is 2 tenths.
canonical_error.why: Confuses grid line boundaries with the actual area columns.

redirect_script.stop: Stop and count the actual columns.
redirect_script.prompt: Point to each shaded column and count it out loud.
redirect_script.praise: Perfect, counting the columns gives the correct fraction.

vocabulary.definition: A grid divided into 10 equal parts.
A grid divided into 100 equal parts.

next_steps.if_fail: Practice counting area segments on a bar model.

sample_items.stem: The bar is divided into 10 equal parts. What fraction of the bar is shaded?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 7/10 counts the unshaded parts; 3/7 compares shaded to unshaded; 1/3 treats the shaded chunk as one of three regions.

skills.item_template: A tenths bar or hundredths grid with some parts shaded. Student names the fraction the model shows. MC with 4 choices; distractors count the unshaded part or flip numerator and denominator.

worked_example_script.text: Draw (or project) a bar split into 10 equal parts with 3 parts shaded.
How many equal parts does the whole bar have? Count them out loud with me.
How many of those parts are shaded? Touch each shaded part as you count.
The total number of equal parts is the bottom number -- the denominator. The shaded count is the top number -- the numerator. So this bar shows 3/10.
If the student says 7/10, they counted the UNSHADED parts. Have them shade-count again with a finger on each shaded piece.
Now show a hundredths grid with 45 squares shaded.
This grid has 100 squares. Do we have to count every shaded square one at a time, or is there a faster way? (Count full rows of 10 first, then leftovers.)
Four full rows is 40, plus 5 more squares. So what fraction of the grid is shaded? What is the denominator, and why is it 100 this time?

skills.name: Write fractions with denominators of 10 or 100 as decimals

prerequisite_skill.description: Write decimals in tenths and hundredths.

skills.i_do_script: Picture a 10-by-10 grid of 100 little squares: 7/10 fills seven whole columns -- 70 little squares -- while 7/100 is just 7 tiny squares. Same digit 7, wildly different amounts, and the decimal we write has to show that difference. When we write a fraction like 7/10 as a decimal, we write it in the tenths place, which is the first spot to the right of the decimal point: 0.7. For 7/100, we need it in the hundredths place: 0.07.

canonical_error.pattern: Places the numerator in the wrong decimal place value.
canonical_error.why: Forgets that the hundredths place is two spots to the right of the decimal.

redirect_script.prompt: Picture the grid first: is 7/100 seven full columns, or seven tiny squares? If the denominator is 100, the last digit must be in the hundredths place. Where does the digit go?

vocabulary.definition: The first place value to the right of the decimal point.
The second place value to the right of the decimal point.

next_steps.if_fail: Review place value charts with decimals.

skills.item_template: A fraction with denominator 10 or 100. Student writes the decimal. Short answer, no choices -- built for timed fluency sprints.

worked_example_script.text: Show a 10-by-10 grid with seven full columns shaded -- that's 7/10, which is 70 of the 100 little squares. Point out how much bigger that is than shading just 7 little squares (7/100). The two fractions are ten times apart, so their decimals cannot look the same.
Write 7/10 on the board, and next to it a place-value chart: ones . tenths hundredths.
Say this fraction out loud. What do we call it? (Seven tenths.)
The name tells us where the digit lives. 'Tenths' is the FIRST spot after the decimal point. So seven tenths is 0.7.
Now write 7/100 right below it.
Say this one out loud. (Seven hundredths.) Is that the same spot as tenths, or a different spot?
If the student writes 0.7 for 7/100, stop -- that is the canonical error. Point at the chart: hundredths is TWO spots to the right, so we need a 0 to hold the tenths place: 0.07.
What about 45/100? Which two places do the 4 and the 5 fill? (0.45 -- the last digit lands in the hundredths place.)
The rule: the place-value NAME of the denominator tells you where the last digit of the numerator must land.

skills.name: Given a model of a percent, choose the equivalent decimal

prerequisite_skill.description: Understand that percent means out of 100.

skills.i_do_script: Percent means per 100, and the hundredths grid shows the whole conversion at once: shade 30 of its 100 squares and you are looking at 30% AND 0.30 -- same shading, two names. Converting a percent to a decimal is dividing by 100, and that's why the digits shift two places: 30% becomes 0.30 (or 0.3). The shift is the shortcut; the grid is why it works. Check every answer against the picture: is the shading more or less than one whole grid?

canonical_error.pattern: Moves the decimal point in the wrong direction or the wrong number of places.
canonical_error.why: Does not divide by 100 to remove the percent sign.

redirect_script.stop: Look at the grid before you move anything.
redirect_script.prompt: Shade the percent on a hundredths grid: is the shading more or less than one whole grid? So should the decimal be more or less than 1? Now divide by 100 and check the shift against the picture.
redirect_script.praise: You checked the decimal against the grid -- the shift means per-100, and you used it that way.

vocabulary.definition: A ratio comparing a number to 100, written with the symbol %.
A way to write a number using place value and a decimal point, like 0.30.

sample_items.stem: The model shows 30%. Which decimal is equivalent to 30%?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 30.0 keeps the percent number as-is; 0.03 moves the decimal three places; 3.00 moves it only one place.

activities.title: Percent-Decimal Partner Sort
materials: One deck of percent and decimal cards per pair
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs sort the cards into matched percent-decimal families.
2. Three trap cards (3.0, 0.03, 0.75) look like they match 30% -- only one decimal card truly matches each percent.
3. A match only counts when the pair can say WHY out loud: '30% means 30 out of 100, and 30/100 is 0.30.'
4. Debrief: which trap card fooled you, and what does it actually equal as a percent?

activities.title: Tia's One-Place Slide
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs read Tia's work and name the exact wrong move.
2. They shade 70 squares on a hundredths grid and ask: does the shading look like 7 wholes (7.0) or less than one whole?
3. Each pair writes the rule in their own words: percent to decimal moves the point how many places, and in which direction?
4. Debrief question: why does 'per 100' force TWO places instead of one?

content.worked_problem: Convert 70% to a decimal. Tia wrote: 70% = 7.0
content.error_step: Tia moved the decimal point only ONE place to the left.
content.why: Percent means per 100, so removing the % sign means dividing by 100 -- two decimal places, not one. 70% = 70/100 = 0.70. A grid check exposes it: 70 shaded squares is less than one whole grid, but 7.0 would be seven whole grids.

activities.title: Grid Flash
activities.instructions:
1. Flash a shaded hundredths grid for 5 seconds (shade full rows so students count rows of 10, not single squares).
2. Students write BOTH the percent and the decimal on whiteboards and hold them up on the count of three.
3. Any split between answers like 0.4 and 0.04 becomes an instant debate: re-show the grid and let the shading referee.
4. Speed round: call out a percent with no grid; students write just the decimal.

strategy_links.why: The hundredths grid is the concrete anchor; CRA moves students from shaded squares to 30/100 to 0.30 without the rule ever being blind.
The one-place-slide error (70% = 7.0) is predictable and highly analyzable -- perfect error-analysis material.
Rapid-fire 'percent means per how many?' choral rounds cement the per-100 reflex this skill runs on.

questioning_prompts: What does the word percent literally mean -- per what?
Look at the grid: is the shaded part more or less than one whole grid? So should your decimal be more or less than 1?
Which direction does the decimal point move when you divide by 100, and how many places?
30% and 0.30 -- point to the part of the grid that shows each one. What do you notice?
If 9% were 0.9, what percent would 0.9 actually be? Check with the grid.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student moves the decimal point in the wrong direction or the wrong number of places -- writes 30% as 3.0 or 30.0.
misconception_redirects.say: Divide the percent value by 100. Which way does the decimal point move?
misconception_redirects.praise: Right! Moving it two places left gives 0.3.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes a single-digit percent like 9% as 0.9 instead of 0.09.
misconception_redirects.say: Nine percent is 9 squares out of 100. Is 0.9 nine squares or ninety squares? Add a zero to hold the tenths place.
misconception_redirects.praise: Exactly -- 0.09 keeps the 9 in the hundredths place, right where 9-out-of-100 lives.

quick_checks.prompt: Write 40% as a decimal, then 4% as a decimal.
quick_checks.look_for: 0.4 and 0.04. If both answers look the same (0.4 twice), the student is dropping digits instead of holding places -- reteach with the grid.

quick_checks.prompt: True or false: 25% = 2.5. Prove it with the grid.
quick_checks.look_for: False -- 25 shaded squares is a quarter of one grid, but 2.5 would be two and a half grids. A student who says true is dividing by 10.

worked_solution.stem: The model shows 30% of the grid shaded. Write the equivalent decimal.

steps.annotation: Percent literally means 'per 100' -- the grid shows exactly that: 30 shaded squares out of 100.
Write the percent as a fraction over 100.
Thirty hundredths: dividing by 100 moves the decimal point TWO places left, so 30 becomes 0.30. The 3 sits in the tenths place, the 0 in the hundredths.

faded_example.stem: The model shows 65% of the grid shaded. Write the equivalent decimal.

steps.annotation: Percent means per 100 -- write it as a fraction over 100.
Divide by 100: which way does the decimal point move, and how many places?
Write the final decimal.

sentence_starters: ___% means ___ out of 100, so the decimal is ___.
I moved the decimal point two places ___ because percent means per ___.

worked_example_script.text: Project a hundredths grid with 30 squares shaded, and write '30%' beside it.
This grid has 100 squares. How many are shaded? So 30% means 30 out of how many?
Percent literally means 'per 100.' So 30% and 30/100 are the same thing -- the grid is a picture of both.
How do we write thirty hundredths as a decimal? Where does the 3 go, and where does the 0 go?
If the student writes 3.0 or 30.0, don't correct -- point at the grid and ask: 'Is the shading more than one whole grid or less? Is 3.0 more than one whole?'
Dividing by 100 moves the decimal point two places to the left: 30 becomes 0.30.
Now shade just 9 squares and write '9%.'
Careful -- this one traps a lot of people. Is 9% equal to 0.9 or 0.09? Use the grid: is 0.9 nine squares or ninety squares?

skills.name: Given a decimal with model, choose the equivalent fraction
skills.i_do_script: To convert a decimal to a fraction, read the decimal using its place value name. For example, 0.25 is twenty-five hundredths, or 25/100. Then simplify by dividing both numbers by their GCF (25), giving 1/4.

canonical_error.pattern: Creates fraction with numerator as denominator or misses simplifying.
canonical_error.why: Confuses decimals with unit fractions, or forgets to simplify.

redirect_script.stop: Read the decimal out loud using place value.
redirect_script.prompt: What place value is the last digit in? Use that as the denominator.

vocabulary.definition: A fraction where the numerator and denominator have no common factors other than 1.
The value of a digit based on its position, like tenths or hundredths.

sample_items.stem: The model shows 0.25. Which fraction is equivalent to 0.25?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1/3 treats 0.25 as 'a quarter-ish unit fraction' guess; 25/10 uses the tenths denominator; 4/1 flips the simplified fraction.

activities.title: Decimal-Fraction Dominoes
materials: Matching card deck: decimals on blue cards, fractions on white cards
activities.instructions:
1. Spread all cards face up. Pairs match each decimal to its equivalent fraction.
2. The decoys are there on purpose: 1/3 does NOT match 0.3, and 1/4 does NOT match 0.4.
3. A match only scores when the pair reads the decimal aloud by its place-value name ('0.3 is three TENTHS, so it's 3/10').
4. Debrief: which decoy almost got you, and how did the place-value name save you?

activities.title: Shade It Three Ways
activities.instructions:
1. Call out a decimal (start with 0.4, then 0.45, then 1.2 using two grids).
2. Students shade the grid to show it, then write the fraction the shading shows, then simplify if they can.
3. Trade papers: partners check that the shading, the decimal, and the fraction all say the same amount.
4. Debrief: for 0.45, why is the denominator 100 and not 10? What in the shading shows that?

activities.title: The Unit-Fraction Trap
activities.instructions:
1. Groups read the flawed work and name the exact wrong move.
2. They shade 0.9 on a hundredths grid, then shade what 1/9 would roughly look like (about 11 squares) -- the pictures don't match.
3. Each group writes the fix-it rule: read the decimal by its place-value name before writing any fraction.
4. Debrief question: what fraction IS 0.9, and how does saying 'nine tenths' out loud hand you the answer?

content.worked_problem: Convert 0.9 to a fraction. A student wrote: 0.9 = 1/9
content.error_step: The student put the 9 in the denominator, turning nine tenths into one ninth.
content.why: 0.9 is read 'nine tenths' -- the 9 counts tenths, so 9 is the numerator and 10 is the denominator: 9/10. One ninth is about 0.11, nowhere near 0.9.

strategy_links.why: Shading grids before writing symbols makes place value visible -- the exact gap behind writing 0.9 as 1/9.
Thinking aloud -- 'I read 0.45 as forty-five hundredths, so my denominator is 100' -- models the read-then-write habit this skill needs.
The unit-fraction confusion (0.3 = 1/3) is a crisp, common bug worth dissecting head-on.

questioning_prompts: Read this decimal out loud using its place-value name. What did you just say -- and what fraction is that?
What place is the LAST digit in? What does that tell you about the denominator?
Is your fraction in simplest form? What number divides evenly into both the top and the bottom?
The grid shows 45 shaded squares. Where do you see the 45 in your fraction? Where do you see the 100?
Could 0.3 and 1/3 be the same number? Shade both on a grid and check.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student creates a fraction with the digit as the denominator (0.3 becomes 1/3) or leaves 25/100 unsimplified.
misconception_redirects.say: What place value is the last digit in? Use that as the denominator.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes 0.45 as 45/10 -- right digits, wrong denominator.
misconception_redirects.say: Read it out loud: is 0.45 forty-five TENTHS or forty-five HUNDREDTHS? The last digit's place names your denominator.
misconception_redirects.praise: That's it -- the 5 sits in the hundredths place, so the denominator is 100.

quick_checks.prompt: Write 0.8 as a fraction, then write 0.08 as a fraction.
quick_checks.look_for: 8/10 (or 4/5) and 8/100 (or 2/25). Identical answers mean the student isn't reading place value -- reteach with the place-value chart.
False -- 0.5 is five tenths, which is 1/2. A 'true' diagnoses the unit-fraction confusion, the skill's canonical error.

worked_solution.stem: The model shows 0.45. Write the equivalent fraction in simplest form.

steps.annotation: The place-value name IS the fraction. The last digit (5) sits in the hundredths place, so the denominator is 100.
The grid agrees: 45 shaded squares out of 100.
Simplify: 5 divides both. 45 / 5 = 9 and 100 / 5 = 20. No number bigger than 1 divides both 9 and 20, so it's in simplest form.

faded_example.stem: The model shows 0.35. Write the equivalent fraction in simplest form.

steps.annotation: The last digit is in the hundredths place, so the denominator is 100.
What number divides evenly into both 35 and 100? Divide both by it.
Write the simplified fraction and check nothing else divides both parts.

sentence_starters: I read 0.___ as ___ (place-value name), so the fraction is ___/___.
I simplified ___/100 by dividing both parts by ___.

worked_example_script.text: Project a hundredths grid with 25 squares shaded, and write '0.25' beside it.
Read this decimal out loud using its place-value name. (Twenty-five hundredths.)
You just SAID the fraction. Twenty-five hundredths is 25 over 100 -- the place-value name always hands you the denominator. The last digit sits in the hundredths place, so the bottom number is 100.
Look at the grid: where do you see the 25? Where do you see the 100?
So we have 25/100. Is that in simplest form? What number divides evenly into BOTH 25 and 100?
Divide both by 25: 25 divided by 25 is 1, and 100 divided by 25 is 4, so 25/100 becomes 1/4. The grid shows it -- 25 squares is exactly one quarter of the whole grid.

Watch here: if the student leaves the answer as 25/100 and calls it done, they've skipped simplifying -- point back and ask 'what number divides both 25 and 100?' If instead they write 1/25, they've flipped numerator and denominator -- have them re-read 0.25 as twenty-five HUNDREDTHS and point to which number names the whole grid; that one is the denominator.
Confirm it: 0.25 = 1/4 in simplest form, and the grid backs it up -- 25 of the 100 squares shaded is the same as 1 of every 4.

skills.name: Choose the fraction equivalent to a given percent
skills.i_do_script: Shade 60 squares of a 100-square grid -- that's 60%. Now bundle the grid into equal chunks of 20 squares: 5 chunks total, and exactly 3 of them are shaded. Nothing was added or removed -- 60 out of 100 and 3 out of 5 are the same picture in bigger pieces. A percent is always a fraction out of 100. 60% is 60/100. Simplify by dividing the numerator and denominator by 20 to get 3/5.

canonical_error.pattern: Fails to simplify the fraction or divides incorrectly.
canonical_error.why: Struggles with division facts or basic fraction reduction.

redirect_script.prompt: Look back at the grid: in chunks of 20 squares, how many chunks are shaded, out of how many chunks total? Divide both numbers by 10 first. Now divide by 2. What fraction do you get?

vocabulary.definition: Fractions that have the same value, even if they look different.
Divide the numerator and denominator by the same number until only 1 divides both.

sample_items.stem: Which fraction is equivalent to 40%?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1/4 is a near-miss benchmark (25%); 40/10 puts the percent over 10 instead of 100; 4/1 drops the place value entirely.

sample_items.stem: Which fraction is equivalent to 60%?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1/6 confuses 60% with a unit fraction; 6/5 puts 60 over 50 badly simplified; 3/50 halves the numerator but not the denominator.

sample_items.stem: Which fraction is equivalent to 25%?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1/25 turns the percent into a unit fraction; 2/5 is 40%, a near benchmark; 25/10 uses the wrong denominator.

sample_items.stem: Which fraction is equivalent to 90%?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1/9 is the unit-fraction confusion; 9/100 keeps the percent digits but the wrong tens place; 10/9 flips the answer.

skills.item_template: A percent (usually a multiple of 5 or 10). Student chooses or writes the equivalent fraction, simplified. MC with 4 choices; distractors put the percent over 10, skip simplifying, or flip the fraction.

practice_problems.stem: Write 50% as a fraction in simplest form.
practice_problems.notes: The friendliest benchmark -- half the grid.

practice_problems.stem: Write 30% as a fraction in simplest form.
Write 25% as a fraction in simplest form.
Write 60% as a fraction in simplest form.
practice_problems.notes: Two simplifying moves: 60/100 -> 6/10 -> 3/5. Stalling at 6/10 is the tell.

practice_problems.stem: Maria converted 40% to a fraction. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: 2/5. In the last step Maria divided the numerator by 2 but forgot to divide the denominator too. Whatever you do to the top you must do to the bottom: 4/10 = 2/5.
practice_problems.notes: Baits the canonical error: simplifying only one part of the fraction.

practice_problems.stem: Write 85% as a fraction in simplest form.
practice_problems.notes: Divide 85/100 by 5 -- not every percent simplifies to a tiny denominator.

practice_problems.stem: Write 5% as a fraction in simplest form.
practice_problems.notes: Less than 10% -- the spec's difficult band.

practice_problems.stem: Write 240% as a mixed number in simplest form.

activities.title: Simplest-Form Speed Sort
materials: Percent cards and fraction cards, one deck per group
activities.instructions:
1. Groups match each percent card to its simplest-form fraction card.
2. The unsimplified decoys (60/100, 4/10) are magnets -- they're equivalent but NOT in simplest form, so they don't score.
3. A match counts only when the group can name the number they divided by to simplify.
4. Debrief: which percent needed TWO rounds of dividing, and how did you know you were done?

activities.title: Percent-Fraction-Grid Threes
materials: Triple card sets: percent, simplest fraction, and 'out of 100' fraction
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs build complete triples: percent, over-100 form, and simplest form (e.g. 80%, 80/100, 4/5).
2. All three must be laid in conversion order: percent -> over 100 -> simplified.
3. A triple scores when the pair reads it as one sentence: '80% is 80 out of 100, which simplifies to 4/5.'
4. Debrief: why does every conversion pass through the over-100 form first?

activities.title: Whiteboard Simplify-Off
activities.instructions:
1. Call out a percent; students write it over 100, simplify fully, and hold up boards on the count of three.
2. Any split between answers like 6/10 and 3/5 becomes a class debate: are they equal? Is either one DONE?
3. Score a point only for simplest form -- equivalent-but-unfinished earns a 'keep going.'
4. End with 5% and 150% to stretch the range.

strategy_links.why: A number talk on 'how many ways can we write 60%?' surfaces the over-100 form and the simplifying chain students need to verbalize.
Whiteboard rounds instantly expose who stalls at 60/100 or halves only the numerator.
Pairing a full correct simplification against Maria's half-simplified 2/10 makes the do-it-to-both-parts rule stick.

questioning_prompts: Every percent starts as a fraction over what number? Write that form first.
What's the biggest number that divides evenly into both the top and the bottom?
You divided the numerator by 2 -- what do you have to do to the denominator?
How do you KNOW your fraction is in simplest form? Convince me.
Is 60/100 wrong? Is it finished? What's the difference?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student fails to simplify the fraction or divides incorrectly -- writes 60% as 6/10 or simplifies to 3/10.
misconception_redirects.say: Divide both numbers by 10 first. Now divide by 2. What fraction do you get?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes the percent over 10 instead of 100 -- 40% becomes 40/10.
misconception_redirects.say: Percent means per HUNDRED. 40/10 is four wholes -- is 40% more than one whole? Rewrite it over 100.
misconception_redirects.praise: Right -- over 100 first, every time. Then simplify.

quick_checks.prompt: Write 20% as a fraction in simplest form.
quick_checks.look_for: 1/5. An answer of 2/10 means the student can convert but stops simplifying; 20/10 means the per-100 idea itself is shaky.

quick_checks.prompt: A classmate says 75% = 75/100 and stops. Is the answer wrong or unfinished? Fix it.
quick_checks.look_for: Unfinished -- 75/100 = 3/4 (divide both by 25). Students who call it 'wrong' need the equivalent-vs-simplest distinction named.

worked_solution.stem: Write 60% as a fraction in simplest form.

steps.annotation: Percent means per 100, so every percent conversion starts by writing the number over 100.
Divide BOTH the top and the bottom by 10. Whatever you do to one part, you do to the other.
Both are still even, so divide both by 2. Nothing bigger than 1 divides both 3 and 5 -- now it's in simplest form.

faded_example.stem: Write 80% as a fraction in simplest form.

steps.annotation: Write the percent over 100 first.
Divide both the numerator and the denominator by the same number.
Keep dividing until nothing bigger than 1 divides both. Write the final fraction.

sentence_starters: ___% is ___ out of 100, which simplifies to ___.
I divided both the top and the bottom by ___ because ___.

worked_example_script.text: Shade 60 of the 100 squares on a hundredths grid and label it 60%.
Now bundle the grid into equal chunks of 20 squares each. How many chunks does the whole grid make? How many of those chunks are shaded?

3 shaded chunks out of 5 chunks -- and not one square changed. That is all simplifying is: regrouping into bigger equal pieces, so the top count AND the bottom count shrink together. If only one of them shrinks, you've changed the picture.
Write '60%' on the board.
Percent means per 100. So before we do anything clever -- what fraction is 60%, straight from the definition?
60/100. Every percent-to-fraction conversion starts exactly here. The only work left is simplifying.
What number divides evenly into BOTH 60 and 100? Start easy -- are they both divisible by 10?
Write 60/100 = 6/10, drawing an arrow labeled 'divide both by 10.'
Are we done? Look at 6 and 10 -- does any number bigger than 1 still divide both?
If the student divides only the numerator (6/10 becomes 3/10), stop them: 'You divided the top by 2 -- what does the bottom need?' The both-parts rule is the whole game.
6/10 = 3/5, and nothing divides both 3 and 5, so 60% = 3/5 in simplest form.

skills.name: Write a decimal as a percent
skills.i_do_script: Percent means per 100, so a decimal in hundredths already IS a percent wearing a different name: 0.45 is 45 hundredths -- 45 per 100 -- which is 45%. Multiplying by 100 just renames hundredths as 'per 100', and that is why the digits shift two places: 0.45 becomes 45%. Check every conversion against the grid: 0.45 shades less than half the grid, and 45% is less than half -- the names agree.

canonical_error.pattern: Moves the decimal point in the wrong direction.

redirect_script.stop: Say the decimal by its place-value name first.
redirect_script.prompt: 0.45 is forty-five HUNDREDTHS -- 45 per 100. Percent means per 100, so what is it as a percent? Check the grid: does your percent shade the same amount as the decimal?
redirect_script.praise: You renamed hundredths as per-100 -- that's what the two-place shift really is.

vocabulary.definition: A ratio comparing a number to 100, written with the symbol %.
To rewrite a number in a different form without changing its value.

sample_items.stem: What is 0.45 written as a percent?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Watch for 0.0045% (moved the decimal left instead of right) or 4.5%.

sample_items.stem: What is 0.125 written as a percent?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Watch for 125% (three places) or 1.25% (one place). The percent keeps a decimal part.

sample_items.stem: What is 0.7 written as a percent?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Watch for 7% -- moving one place instead of two.

sample_items.stem: What is 0.06 written as a percent?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Watch for 60% (misreading 0.06 as 0.6) or 0.06%.

skills.item_template: A decimal (terminating, including thousandths like 0.125). Student writes the equivalent percent. Numeric response with a % sign after the answer box.

practice_problems.stem: Write 0.5 as a percent.
practice_problems.notes: Anchor to the benchmark: half of the grid is 50%.

practice_problems.stem: Write 0.25 as a percent.
Write 0.45 as a percent.
Write 0.06 as a percent.
practice_problems.notes: Hundredths with a leading zero -- 60% is the trap.

practice_problems.stem: Jordan converted 0.32 to a percent. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: To make a percent, move the decimal point two places
practice_problems.answer: 32%. Jordan moved the decimal point two places in the WRONG direction -- he divided by 100 instead of multiplying. Decimal to percent multiplies by 100: 0.32 x 100 = 32, so 0.32 = 32%.
practice_problems.notes: Baits the canonical error: moving the decimal point the wrong way.

practice_problems.stem: Write 0.125 as a percent.
practice_problems.notes: The percent itself keeps a decimal -- students often 'finish' at 125%.

practice_problems.stem: Write 1.3 as a percent.
practice_problems.notes: Greater than one whole means greater than 100%.

practice_problems.stem: Write 0.007 as a percent.
practice_problems.notes: Less than 1% -- the two-places-right rule still holds exactly.

activities.title: Decimal-Percent Pairs
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs match each decimal to its percent. The decoys punish one-place moves: 0.4 does NOT match 4%.
2. A match scores only with the sentence: '0.4 x 100 = 40, so 0.4 is 40%.'
3. Sort the finished pairs from least to greatest as a bonus -- 0.007 to 1.3.
4. Debrief: which pair proves that a decimal LESS than 0.01 makes a percent less than 1%?

activities.title: Jordan's Wrong-Way Move
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs read Jordan's work and name the exact wrong move.
2. Sanity check: shade 0.32 on a grid -- about a third of the squares. Could a third of a grid be 0.0032% of it?
3. Pairs write the direction rule in their own words, including WHY (percent counts hundredths, so you multiply by 100).
4. Debrief: which direction makes the number look bigger, and which conversion goes that way?

content.worked_problem: Convert 0.32 to a percent. Jordan wrote: 0.32 = 0.0032%
content.error_step: Jordan moved the decimal point two places LEFT (divided by 100) instead of two places right.
content.why: A percent counts hundredths, so decimal-to-percent multiplies by 100: 0.32 x 100 = 32%. The grid check: 0.32 is 32 shaded squares out of 100 -- clearly 32%, not a hair above zero percent.

activities.title: Two-Places-Right Showdown
activities.instructions:
1. Call out a decimal (start with 0.4, then 0.45, then 0.06, then 1.5); students write the percent and hold boards up on three.
2. Any split (6% vs 60% for 0.06) becomes a debate: shade it on a hundredths grid and let the squares referee.
3. Reverse round: call a percent, students write the decimal -- direction is the whole skill.
4. Track 'traps that split the room' for tomorrow's warm-up.

strategy_links.why: Call-response rounds ('decimal to percent -- which way? RIGHT. How many places? TWO.') automate the direction decision.
Whiteboard passes catch wrong-direction moves (0.32 to 0.0032%) the moment they happen.
The wrong-direction bug is systematic, not careless -- analyzing it directly beats re-drilling the rule.

questioning_prompts: Decimal to percent -- are we multiplying by 100 or dividing by 100? How do you know?
Should the percent number look bigger or smaller than the decimal? Why?
0.45 -- shade it on a grid. How many squares? So what percent?
Where does the decimal point end up in 0.125 x 100? Can a percent have a decimal in it?
What percent would 1.0 be? So what must 1.3 be, before you even compute?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student moves the decimal point in the wrong direction -- writes 0.45 as 0.0045%.
misconception_redirects.say: Move the decimal point two places to the RIGHT. Where does it go?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student moves only one place -- writes 0.7 as 7%.
misconception_redirects.say: Percent means hundredths, and multiplying by 100 moves TWO places. Count the jumps with your pencil: 0.7 to 7 to 70.
misconception_redirects.praise: That's it -- two jumps right lands on 70%.

quick_checks.prompt: Write 0.9 as a percent, then 0.09 as a percent.
quick_checks.look_for: 90% and 9%. Matching answers mean place value is collapsing; a 0.009% means the direction rule is inverted.

quick_checks.prompt: Which is greater: 0.8 or 75%? Prove it by converting one of them.
quick_checks.look_for: 0.8 = 80% > 75%. Students who can't compare across forms are converting mechanically without meaning.

worked_solution.stem: What is 0.45 written as a percent?

steps.annotation: Read the decimal by place value: forty-five hundredths -- 45 out of 100.
Percent MEANS per 100, so 45 out of 100 is 45% by definition.
Multiplying by 100 moves the decimal point two places to the RIGHT. Decimal to percent always goes right; percent to decimal goes left.

faded_example.stem: What is 0.06 written as a percent?

steps.annotation: Six hundredths -- 6 out of 100.
Per 100 IS percent. Write it with the % sign -- careful, is it 6% or 60%?

sentence_starters: I multiplied by 100 and moved the decimal point two places ___, so 0.___ = ___%.
The percent should look ___ than the decimal because percent counts hundredths.

worked_example_script.text: Write '0.45' on the board next to a hundredths grid with 45 squares shaded.
Read this decimal by its place-value name. (Forty-five hundredths.) So it's 45 out of how many?
Percent MEANS per 100. If 0.45 is 45 out of 100, then it's 45% -- we barely had to do anything.
Here's the shortcut version: 0.45 times 100 equals what? Which way did the decimal point move, and how many places?
If the student moves the point LEFT (0.0045), pause and point at the grid: 'Is 0.45 almost half the grid? Is 0.0045% almost half?' The size check catches the direction error every time.
Write '0.06' below it.
Same move: 0.06 times 100. Is that 6% or 60%? Count the two jumps with your pencil.
One more: 0.125. Move two places right. Can a percent have a decimal point left in it? What do you get?

skills.name: Select two values equivalent to a given percent

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiple representations of equivalent rational numbers.

skills.i_do_script: For this skill, we find both the decimal and simplified fraction that are equivalent to the percent. For example, 75% = 0.75 and 75/100 = 3/4.

canonical_error.pattern: Only selects one correct equivalent value or selects incorrect models.
canonical_error.why: Inverts fractions or stops working after finding the first match.

redirect_script.stop: This is a select two question.
redirect_script.prompt: Find the equivalent decimal first. Now find the equivalent fraction. Check both.
redirect_script.praise: Great work finding both equivalent values.

vocabulary.definition: Having the same value, even when written in a different form.
The amount a number represents, no matter how it is written.

sample_items.stem: Select the two values that are equivalent to 60%.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1/6 is the unit-fraction confusion; 6/1 drops the per-100 meaning; 0.06 moves the decimal one place too far.

sample_items.stem: Select the two values that are equivalent to 25%.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4/1 inverts the fraction; 2.5 moves the decimal only one place; 1/25 turns the percent into a unit fraction.

sample_items.stem: Select the two values that are equivalent to 7/8.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 0.8 rounds the division too early; 8.75% and 875% move the decimal the wrong number of places when converting to percent.

sample_items.stem: Select the two values that are equivalent to 0.4.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4% moves one place instead of two; 1/4 confuses 0.4 with a quarter; 0.04 shifts the decimal's own place value.

skills.item_template: A percent (or a fraction/decimal). Student selects the TWO equivalent values from five choices mixing fractions and decimals. Multi-select; distractors invert the fraction or shift the decimal point.

practice_problems.stem: Write 75% as a decimal.
Write 0.2 as a fraction in simplest form.
Write two values equivalent to 40%: one decimal and one fraction in simplest form.
practice_problems.notes: The produce-both demand is the heart of this skill -- don't accept just one.

practice_problems.stem: Which two are equivalent to 0.6: 6%, 60%, 3/5, 1/6?
practice_problems.notes: One percent trap (6%) and one unit-fraction trap (1/6) in the same set.

practice_problems.stem: Amir picked two values equivalent to 80%. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: 0.8 and 4/5. Amir's decimal was right, but he flipped the fraction: 8/10 simplifies to 4/5, not 5/4. 5/4 is 125% -- more than one whole, while 80% is less than one whole.
practice_problems.notes: Baits the canonical error: inverting the fraction on the second equivalent.

practice_problems.stem: Complete the table so every row shows the same value three ways.
practice_problems.notes: The completed first row is the worked model; each ? must agree with its whole row.

practice_problems.stem: Write 7/8 as a decimal AND as a percent.
practice_problems.notes: Divide 7 by 8 first; the percent keeps a decimal part.

practice_problems.stem: The double number line pairs fractions with percents. What percent lines up with 3/4, and what fraction lines up with 25%?
practice_problems.answer: 3/4 lines up with 75%; 25% lines up with 1/4.
practice_problems.notes: The double number line shows equivalence as position: same spot, same value.

activities.title: Three-Way Value Match
materials: Card sets in three colors: fractions, decimals, percents
activities.instructions:
1. Groups build complete triples: fraction, decimal, and percent naming the SAME value (e.g. 3/5, 0.6, 60%).
2. Two trap cards (1/6 and 6%) look like they belong with the 0.6 family -- they don't.
3. A triple scores only when the group reads all three aloud as one value: 'three fifths, zero point six, sixty percent -- same number, three costumes.'
4. Debrief: which representation did your group convert THROUGH to check the others?

activities.title: Build a Double Number Line
materials: Long strip of paper per pair
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs draw one long line, mark 0% and 100% at the ends, then tick 25%, 50%, 75% on top.
2. Below the SAME line they place sticky notes with fractions (1/4, 1/2, 3/4) and decimals (0.25, 0.5, 0.75) at the matching spots.
3. Challenge round: place 3/5, 0.6, and 60% -- all three must land on the same spot, between 50% and 75%.
4. Debrief: what does it mean when two numbers share a spot on the line?

activities.title: Equivalent or Impostor?
materials: Claim cards, one set per pair
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs sort claim cards into 'Equivalent' and 'Impostor.'
2. Every impostor must be FIXED: write the value it actually equals.
3. Fastest check wins style points: convert both sides to the same form and compare.
4. Debrief: which impostor fooled you longest, and which conversion exposed it?

strategy_links.why: Multi-select demands justifying BOTH picks -- partners must convince each other before committing, which surfaces the stop-after-one-match habit.
The double number line is the representational bridge that shows all three forms occupying one position -- one value.
A number talk on 'name 60% as many ways as you can' builds the flexible multi-representation fluency this skill assesses.

questioning_prompts: You found one match -- how many does the question ask for? What form is missing?
Convert everything to the same form first. Which form is fastest to compare in?
Is 5/4 more or less than one whole? Is 80% more or less than one whole? So can they match?
Where would 0.6 and 3/5 sit on the number line? What does sharing a spot tell you?
Before checking any choices: what SHOULD the decimal and fraction for 45% be?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student selects only one correct equivalent value, or picks an inverted fraction like 4/3 for 75%.
misconception_redirects.say: Find the equivalent decimal first. Now find the equivalent fraction. Check both.
misconception_redirects.praise: Great work finding both equivalent values.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student picks a decimal with the point shifted -- 0.06 as a match for 60%.
misconception_redirects.say: Is 60% more than half or less than half? Now, is 0.06 more than half? Size-check every choice before you commit.
misconception_redirects.praise: Nice -- the size check threw out the impostor instantly.

quick_checks.prompt: Name 50% two other ways -- one fraction, one decimal.
quick_checks.look_for: 1/2 and 0.5. Producing only one form, or 5/10 with no simplification, shows the coordination is still one-directional.

quick_checks.prompt: True or false: 0.8 and 4/5 and 80% are all the same value. How do you know?
quick_checks.look_for: True, with a conversion chain (4/5 = 80/100 = 0.8 = 80%) -- not just 'they look right.'

worked_solution.stem: Select the two values that are equivalent to 60%: 1/6, 3/5, 6/1, 0.6, 0.06.

steps.annotation: Find the decimal first: divide by 100, moving the point two places left. That matches 0.6 -- and rules out 0.06, which moved three places.
Now the fraction: write 60 over 100 and simplify (divide both by 20). That matches 3/5.
1/6 is about 17%, and 6/1 is 600% -- both fail the size check. The two answers are 3/5 and 0.6.

faded_example.stem: Select the two values that are equivalent to 40%: 1/4, 2/5, 4/1, 0.4, 0.04.

steps.annotation: Decimal first: divide by 100, two places left.
Now the fraction: write 40 over 100 and simplify. Which choice matches?
Size-check the leftovers to make sure they fail, then name your two answers.

sentence_starters: The decimal for ___% is ___, and the fraction is ___, because both mean ___ out of 100.
I ruled out ___ because it is (bigger/smaller) than one whole and ___% is not.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'Select the TWO values equivalent to 60%: 1/6, 3/5, 6/1, 0.6, 0.06.'
Before touching the choices -- what should the decimal for 60% be? Work it out first.
And what should the fraction be? Start from 60 over 100 and simplify.
Now we shop with a list: we're looking for 0.6 and 3/5. Predicting first means the traps can't pull us around.
Is 0.06 the same as 0.6? Size-check it: 60% is more than half -- is 0.06 more than half?
What about 1/6? It has a 6 in it. Is one-sixth anywhere near 60%?
The classic miss is stopping after one correct pick. If the student circles 0.6 and stops, ask: 'How many does the question want? You have the decimal -- where's the fraction?'
The answers are 3/5 and 0.6 -- one value, two costumes. Digits that LOOK alike (6, 0.06, 1/6, 6/1) are not the same value.

skills.name: Convert a repeating decimal to its equivalent fraction
skills.i_do_script: Repeating decimals like 0.333... can be written as fractions. 0.333... is equivalent to 1/3. 0.111... is equivalent to 1/9.

canonical_error.pattern: Treats repeating decimals as terminating decimals.
canonical_error.why: Does not understand that the pattern goes on forever and doesn't end at the thousandths place.

redirect_script.stop: This decimal has '...' indicating it repeats forever.
redirect_script.prompt: Recall the repeating fraction family for ninths or thirds. What is the denominator?

vocabulary.definition: A decimal with a digit or group of digits that repeats forever.
A decimal that ends, like 0.25 -- it does not repeat forever.

sample_items.stem:
What is the decimal equivalent of 8/11?

If the decimal repeats, write the first 4 decimal places followed by "..."
sample_items.distractor_logic: Watch for 0.72 (stops too early, treating it as terminating) or 1.375 (divided 11 by 8).

sample_items.stem:
What is the decimal equivalent of 5/6?

If the decimal repeats, write the first 4 decimal places followed by "..."
sample_items.distractor_logic: Watch for 5.6 (mashing the digits together) or 0.8888... (repeating the wrong digit -- here only the 3 repeats).

sample_items.stem: Which fraction is equivalent to 0.111...?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1/10 treats it as the terminating decimal 0.1; 111/1000 cuts the repeat off at three digits; 1/3 confuses the ninths family (0.111... is 1/9, while 1/3 is 0.333...).

sample_items.stem: Which fraction is equivalent to 0.2727...?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 27/100 treats the repeating decimal as the terminating 0.27; 2/7 is a nearby repeater (0.2857...) from the wrong family; 1/27 inverts into a unit fraction.

sample_items.stem: Two students convert 5/6 to a decimal. Student 1 says 5/6 = 5.6. Student 2 says 5/6 = 0.8333... Which student is correct, and why?
sample_items.answer: Student 2. Converting a fraction means DIVIDING the numerator by the denominator: 5 / 6 = 0.8333..., where the 3 repeats forever. Student 1 just pushed the two digits together, and 5.6 is greater than 1 while 5/6 is less than 1.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who side with Student 1 are reading the fraction bar as a decimal point instead of as division.

skills.item_template: A fraction whose decimal repeats (thirds, sixths, ninths, sevenths, elevenths, twelfths). Student divides to find the repeating decimal, writing the first 4 decimal places followed by '...' -- or identifies the fraction for a given repeating decimal. Numeric response or MC.

practice_problems.stem: Write 1/3 as a decimal. If it repeats, write the first 4 decimal places followed by "..."
practice_problems.notes: The friendliest repeater -- most students already know it.

practice_problems.stem: Which fraction is equivalent to 0.111...?
practice_problems.notes: Introduce the ninths family: 0.111... = 1/9, 0.222... = 2/9, and so on.

practice_problems.stem: Write 2/3 as a decimal. If it repeats, write the first 4 decimal places followed by "..."
Write 5/6 as a decimal. If it repeats, write the first 4 decimal places followed by "..."
practice_problems.notes: The first digit (8) does NOT repeat -- only the 3 does. This is the spec's difficult wrinkle.

practice_problems.stem: Lena converted 0.666... to a fraction. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: 2/3. The '...' means the 6s never stop -- the decimal does NOT end at the thousandths place. 666/1000 is the terminating decimal 0.666 exactly, which is slightly less than 0.666... The repeating decimal 0.666... is exactly 2/3.
practice_problems.notes: Baits the canonical error: treating a repeating decimal as if it terminates.

practice_problems.stem: Write 8/11 as a decimal. If it repeats, write the first 4 decimal places followed by "..."
practice_problems.notes: A two-digit repeating block -- the pattern is 72, not a single digit.

practice_problems.stem: Write 1/7 as a decimal. If it repeats, write the first 4 decimal places followed by "..."
practice_problems.notes: The repeating block (142857) is six digits long -- students only report the first four places.

practice_problems.stem: Which is greater: 0.666... or 0.66? Explain how you know.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-why stretch: the '...' carries real value.

activities.title: The Decimal That Wouldn't End
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs read Lena's work and name the exact wrong move.
2. They run the long division for 2 / 3 and watch the remainder: it's ALWAYS 2, so the 6s can never stop.
3. Pairs write the rule: what does '...' promise about the digits, and why can't 666/1000 keep that promise?
4. Debrief: how does the remainder in long division tell you a decimal will repeat forever?

content.worked_problem: Convert 0.666... to a fraction. Lena wrote: 0.666... = 666/1000
content.error_step: Lena cut the repeating decimal off after three digits and treated it as a terminating decimal.
content.why: The '...' means the 6s continue forever -- the number is strictly greater than 0.666. In the long division 2 / 3, the remainder is always 2, so the quotient digit 6 recurs endlessly: 0.666... is exactly 2/3.

activities.title: Repeater Families
materials: Fraction cards and decimal cards, one deck per group
activities.instructions:
1. Groups sort decimal cards under their fraction families: ninths (single digit repeats), thirds/sixths (watch the non-repeating first digit), and elevenths (two-digit blocks).
2. Terminating decoys (0.25, 0.375) go in a 'does not repeat' pile.
3. A card scores only when the group can SAY the pattern: 'for 5/6, only the 3 repeats -- the 8 happens once.'
4. Debrief: which family repeats a two-digit block, and how could you spot it without dividing?

activities.title: Divide and Discover
activities.instructions:
1. Students long-divide three fractions: 3/4 (terminates), 1/3 (repeats immediately), 1/6 (repeats AFTER one non-repeating digit).
2. At each step they circle the remainder. The discovery: a remainder of 0 means the decimal stops; a remainder you've seen before means the digits will repeat from there.
3. Students annotate each result: 'terminates' or 'repeats, pattern = ___.'
4. Debrief: without dividing, predict whether 5/6 terminates -- then check.

strategy_links.why: Setting Student 2's correct division against Student 1's digit-mashing (5/6 vs 5.6) is exactly the justification move the above-proficiency band demands.
Thinking aloud through the long division -- 'the remainder is 2 again, so this digit will repeat forever' -- makes the repetition visible instead of magical.
'Which student is correct and why?' prompts are built for pair debate before committing to a written justification.

questioning_prompts: What operation does the fraction bar tell you to do? So what division do you set up for 5/6?
What does the '...' at the end of 0.8333... promise about the digits?
Look at your remainder -- have you seen it before? What does that tell you about the digits coming next?
In 0.8333..., which digit repeats and which digit happens only once?
Is 5/6 more or less than 1? Is 5.6 more or less than 1? What does that tell you?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student treats a repeating decimal as terminating -- writes 0.333... as 333/1000.
misconception_redirects.say: Recall the repeating fraction family for ninths or thirds. What is the denominator?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student converts 5/6 by pushing the digits together into 5.6 instead of dividing.
misconception_redirects.say: The fraction bar means DIVIDE. Is 5/6 bigger or smaller than 1? Is 5.6 bigger or smaller than 1? Now divide 5 by 6 and see what you get.
misconception_redirects.praise: That's the move -- divide the top by the bottom, and the size check confirms it.

quick_checks.prompt: Write 1/3 and 1/4 as decimals. Which one repeats?
quick_checks.look_for: 0.333... repeats; 0.25 terminates. A student who writes 0.33 with no dots is still cutting repeaters off.

quick_checks.prompt: In the decimal for 1/6, which digit repeats forever?
quick_checks.look_for: The 6 (0.1666...) -- and the 1 happens once. Saying 'the 1 and the 6' means the non-repeating-first-digit idea needs the long-division walk-through.

worked_solution.stem: What is the decimal equivalent of 5/6? If the decimal repeats, write the first 4 decimal places followed by "..."

steps.annotation: The fraction bar is a division sign: divide the numerator by the denominator.
After the first step the remainder is ALWAYS 2 -- so the digit 3 will repeat forever. The 8 happens only once.
Write the first 4 decimal places and '...' to show the 3 repeats. Size check: 5/6 is a little less than 1, and 0.8333... is a little less than 1.

faded_example.stem: What is the decimal equivalent of 4/9? If the decimal repeats, write the first 4 decimal places followed by "..."

steps.annotation: The fraction bar means divide. Watch the remainder.
The remainder is 4 again -- what does that tell you about the next digits?
Write the first 4 decimal places followed by '...'

sentence_starters: The remainder repeated, so the digit ___ will repeat forever, and the decimal is ___.
Student ___ is correct because the fraction bar means ___, and the size check shows ___.

worked_example_script.text: Write '5/6' on the board and the claim from two students: Student 1 says 5.6, Student 2 says 0.8333...
Before any math: is 5/6 more than 1 or less than 1? Which student's answer is even possible?
The fraction bar is a division sign. Converting 5/6 to a decimal means dividing 5 by 6 -- not pushing the digits together.
Set up the long division 5 / 6 and work it step by step, circling each remainder.
First digit: 50 divided by 6 is 8, remainder 2. Next: 20 divided by 6 is 3, remainder 2. What just happened with the remainder?
This is the aha: the remainder is 2 AGAIN, so the next digit must be 3 again, forever. If the student wants to 'finish' the division, ask what would have to happen for it to stop (a remainder of 0).
So which digit repeats forever, and which digit happened only once? How do we write that answer? (0.8333...)
Now you be the judge: explain in one sentence why Student 2 is right and Student 1 is wrong.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

progression.narrative: 6.RP.1 asks students to move freely between the three costumes a positive rational number can wear -- fraction, decimal, and percent -- without a calculator. Everything rests on one idea: percent means 'per 100,' and the hundredths grid makes all three names visible at once (30 shaded squares IS 30/100 IS 0.30 IS 30%). The progression starts there: read a shaded model and name it as a decimal (S1) or a fraction (S2), so the conversions are anchored to a picture before they become a rule. Then the model comes away and students convert symbolically: percent to simplified fraction (S3) and decimal to percent (S4), the two moves where the 'out of 100' idea does all the work. At proficiency the standard demands coordination -- naming the SAME value in more than one way at once (S5), selecting both the decimal and the fraction equivalent to a given percent. Finally the numbers stop cooperating: fractions like 5/6 and 8/11 divide into decimals that never end (S6), and students must recognize, write, and defend repeating decimals -- the bridge to 7th-grade proportional reasoning.

steps.rationale: Anchor 'percent means per 100' to a picture: a shaded hundredths grid IS the percent and IS the decimal at the same time. Reading the model before applying a rule keeps the two-place decimal shift from becoming a blind trick.

Read the same models as fractions: place value names the denominator (0.45 is forty-five hundredths, 45/100). This is the second leg of the model-based tripod and the last place the grid is provided for the student.
Drop the model: convert a percent to a fraction symbolically -- write it over 100, then simplify. Simplifying is where this step earns its place; 60% must become 3/5, not stall at 60/100.

Convert in the direction students most often botch: decimal to percent means multiplying by 100 (two places RIGHT), the mirror image of S1. Doing both directions back-to-back is what makes the movement a decision instead of a habit.

The standard's at-proficiency demand: name one value more than one way at once. Given 60%, a student must produce BOTH 0.6 and 3/5 -- coordination across all three representations, not a single memorized hop.

Extend conversion to fractions whose decimals never terminate (5/6, 8/11). Students divide numerator by denominator, recognize the repeating pattern, write it correctly, and justify why 5/6 is 0.8333... and not 5.6 -- the standard's above-proficiency justification demand.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S5 (name a percent two ways at once) -- if they pass, jump to S6 (repeating decimals). If they fail, check whether the gap is reading models (S1/S2) before testing the symbolic conversions (S3/S4). This avoids walking all six skills when the student may only need one or two.
